1.name: Kamoni Williams
1.about: A true generational prospect, Williams combines extraordinary physical dimensions with a level of two-way skill almost unheard of for a 7'3" center. His 7'9" wingspan makes him a dominant rim protector, while his handle, passing vision and multi-level scoring allow him to legitimately run offense. He changes games on both ends and possesses the rare ceiling of a player capable of becoming the centerpiece of an NBA franchise.

2.name: Miro Sanderson
2.about: One of the premier prospects in the class, Sanderson pairs legitimate lead-guard playmaking with advanced defensive instincts and reliable perimeter shooting at 6'6". He controls tempo, consistently creates quality looks for teammates and uses his length to disrupt opposing guards without relying on elite athleticism. His unusually complete two-way skill set against professional competition gives him legitimate franchise-guard upside.

3.name: Kione Anthony
3.about: One of the most complete guards in the class, Anthony immediately established himself as a two-way difference-maker at UConn. His combination of size, explosiveness and a 7'0" wingspan allows him to pressure the rim, defend multiple perimeter positions and create turnovers, while his developing pull-up game and playmaking add legitimate offensive upside. He projects as a high-ceiling NBA guard with few glaring physical limitations.

4.name: Hunter Hutchinson
4.about: After spending his first two seasons at Georgia, Hutchinson transferred to Michigan and elevated his draft stock with a highly productive junior campaign. His combination of perimeter shooting, touch and polished footwork makes him one of the class’s most skilled offensive bigs, capable of scoring from several areas of the floor. Athletic and defensive limitations remain concerns, but his advanced offensive repertoire gives him considerable upside.

5.name: Olavi Metsälä
5.about: Heavily recruited out of Finland, Metsälä arrived at UConn with enormous expectations after entering the preseason viewed as a potential top-two selection. His freshman year reinforced much of the appeal, as his floor spacing, athletic finishing and weak-side rim protection give him an unusually complete foundation for a modern big. Questions surrounding his strength and individual creation have cooled some of the early hype, but he remains one of the class’s premier two-way talents.

6.name: Cameron Moya
6.about: A uniquely skilled oversized guard, Moya established himself as one of the class’s most versatile freshmen at Illinois. At 6'7", he sees over defenses as a facilitator, consistently spaces the floor from three and uses his length and instincts to generate turnovers defensively. His lack of burst limits his rim pressure, but his combination of shooting, passing and defensive anticipation gives him considerable two-way value.

7.name: Kamren Thomson
7.about: Thomson overwhelms opponents with an imposing blend of power, length and explosiveness rarely found in a 260-pound center. He establishes deep position, punishes defenders through contact and attacks the offensive glass, while his 7'3" wingspan and surprising mobility make him a disruptive interior defender. His nonexistent perimeter game limits his offensive range, but his ability to physically control the paint gives him substantial two-way value.

8.name: Youssouf Toledano
8.about: Few prospects in the class possess Toledano’s combination of explosiveness, strength and open-floor speed. He attacks gaps aggressively, powers through contact and can finish well above the rim, with his 6'11" wingspan adding another dimension around the basket and defensively. His physical upside is among the best in the draft, but his jumper and overall offensive polish remain the primary swing skills.

9.name: Marteese Jefferson
9.about: Once projected as a top-five pick, Jefferson remains one of the class’s most talented perimeter scorers despite sliding slightly down the board. His combination of shooting range, pull-up creation and off-ball movement gives him considerable offensive upside, while his 6'11" wingspan provides encouraging defensive tools. Continued growth as a playmaker and finisher could easily help him outperform his current draft slot.

10.name: Eliott Tissot
10.about: Tissot has emerged as one of the class’s most intriguing young international bigs, combining exceptional length with a surprisingly versatile offensive game. He can space the floor, attack slower defenders and create opportunities within the flow of the offense, while his 7'3" wingspan gives him considerable defensive upside. He’s still developing physically and can be inconsistent possession to possession, but his combination of skill, length and youth gives him one of the stronger ceilings in the class.

11.name: Hashujani Maliffeno
11.about: Maliffeno presents an unusual combination of power, shooting and explosiveness for a 249-pound big. He can pull opposing centers away from the basket with legitimate three-point range, then punish hard closeouts with forceful drives and above-the-rim finishes. His 7'2" wingspan helps offset his lack of traditional center height, though improving his defensive discipline and interior positioning will be important against NBA frontcourts.

12.name: Colby Lewis
12.about: Playing on a loaded UConn roster, Lewis didn’t need to dominate the ball to establish himself as one of the class’s better scoring prospects. He consistently made the most of his opportunities, attacking closeouts, creating smooth midrange looks and finishing creatively around the basket. His versatility alongside other high-level talent strengthens his projection as a scorer capable of fitting into different NBA lineups.

13.name: Sky Lewis Jr.
13.about: A polished scoring guard, Lewis elevated his draft stock with a breakout junior season at Murray State. He thrives creating off the dribble, using changes of pace and sharp footwork to reach pull-up opportunities from both the midrange and beyond the arc. His scoring craft gives him legitimate first-round appeal, though average athleticism and inconsistent defensive impact place more pressure on his offensive production.

14.name: Alijah Barnett
14.about: Still just 19 despite completing his sophomore season, Barnett already looks like one of the class’s most impactful defensive forwards. His 7'3" wingspan allows him to erase shots from unexpected angles, disrupt passing lanes and switch across multiple positions. Continued progress as a spot-up shooter gives him a legitimate path toward becoming a high-level two-way NBA forward.

15.name: Yorell Johnson
15.about: One of the class’s premier shooting forwards, Johnson capped his Wichita State career by consistently stretching defenses well beyond the arc. At 6'8", he shoots comfortably over contests, relocates effectively and requires very little offensive maintenance. His athletic limitations lower the ceiling, but his combination of size and elite shooting gives him a highly translatable NBA skill.

16.name: Brandon Ashford
16.about: Ashford arrived at Texas with a mature interior scoring package and quickly proved capable of generating offense from the post. His powerful 249-pound frame, long arms and advanced footwork allow him to establish position, counter defenders and finish with touch using either power or finesse. Limited athleticism and virtually no floor-spacing ability create questions about his NBA fit, but his post skill gives him a legitimate offensive foundation.

17.name: Jarrah Blackwell
17.about: Blackwell has carved out a clear identity against professional competition with his physicality, interior finishing and relentless work around the basket. His powerful 234-pound frame allows him to establish position, punish switches and finish through contact, while his length and motor make him productive on the glass. The complete absence of a perimeter game limits his offensive flexibility, but his strength and interior presence give him a strong foundation as a physical NBA big.

18.name: Justus Williams
18.about: Arriving at Duke as a five-star, top-10 recruit, Williams quickly demonstrated one of the more polished scoring packages among the class’s young wings. His mature frame, footwork and touch allow him to manufacture offense inside the arc, while a respectable jumper adds another dimension. Continued development as a creator for others could unlock considerably more offensive upside.

19.name: Simon Kaminskas
19.about: A dependable two-way presence at Illinois, Kaminskas has developed into one of the safer complementary forwards in the class. His strong frame allows him to handle physical assignments across multiple positions, while his left-handed jumper provides reliable floor spacing. He may never become a high-volume creator, but his shooting, defense and versatility give him a straightforward NBA fit.

20.name: Jordon Waters
20.about: A five-star recruit entering BYU, Waters backed up much of his reputation by flashing an exciting combination of explosiveness, length and defensive potential. He’s dangerous attacking the rim, cutting and running in transition, with enough physical tools to eventually defend multiple positions. His jumper and half-court creation remain works in progress, but there’s substantial two-way upside if those skills develop.

21.name: Carson Williams Jr.
21.about: One of the two best perimeter defenders in the class, Williams made an immediate impact at Kansas with relentless ball pressure and an ability to disrupt opposing guards. His 6'9" wingspan, strong frame and quick reactions allow him to navigate screens and generate turnovers, while his power gives him value attacking downhill. Developing a reliable jumper remains the key to unlocking a larger NBA role.

22.name: Sam Schmitz
22.about: Four years of college experience have turned Schmitz into one of the class’s most polished perimeter scorers. At 6'7", he combines high-level movement shooting with enough pull-up ability to punish aggressive closeouts and create occasional offense himself. His athletic limitations are significant, but his size, shooting versatility and advanced offensive feel give him a clear NBA role.

23.name: Tucker Davis
23.about: Davis has developed into one of the more skilled offensive bigs in the college game, using his shooting touch and feel to compensate for an underwhelming physical profile. He can stretch defenses beyond the arc, operate from the elbows and attack mismatches with controlled footwork. His lack of size and athleticism for an NBA frontcourt role creates legitimate defensive concerns, but his shooting and offensive polish give him a clear pathway to contributing.

24.name: Darius Hall
24.about: Hall made an immediate impact at Auburn through sheer power, length and activity around the basket. His 240-pound frame and 7'2" wingspan make him a punishing interior finisher, active offensive rebounder and imposing presence around the rim. His offensive game outside the paint is extremely limited, but his youth and combination of strength, length and athleticism leave considerable room for development.

25.name: Ja’Kaih Ellington
25.about: Ellington’s combination of explosiveness, strength and defensive activity made him an immediate frontcourt weapon during his freshman season at Alabama. He flies to the rim as a lob target, covers ground quickly as a help defender and uses his 7'0" wingspan to challenge shots above the basket. His offensive skill set remains narrow, but his athletic tools give him significant upside as an energetic two-way big.

26.name: Tyler Bridges
26.about: After beginning his career at Michigan State, Bridges found his footing at Arizona and developed into a powerful, explosive two-way wing. His 223-pound frame and vertical pop make him dangerous downhill and in transition, while an improved jumper has made him more functional in the half court. His physical tools and finishing provide a strong foundation even if his creation remains limited.

27.name: Elio Tchouaméni
27.about: Experience against French professional competition has helped shape Tchouaméni into an intriguing combo guard with a blend of scoring and playmaking ability. He uses his long 6'9" wingspan effectively on both ends, showing patience in pick-and-roll situations and enough creation ability to function at either guard spot. He remains somewhat streaky as a shooter and lacks elite burst, but his versatility gives him a realistic pathway as a rotational combo guard.

28.name: Karif Njepchiru
28.about: Njepchiru established himself as a disruptive two-way big at Colorado State, using his enormous 7'3" wingspan and mobility to protect the paint, switch onto different matchups and create havoc defensively. Offensively, he thrives as a rim runner and powerful finisher rather than a featured scorer. His shooting and creation remain limited, but his defensive versatility gives him a strong NBA calling card.

29.name: Eliyah Morris
29.about: Few guards in the class can match Morris’ combination of size, power and explosiveness. The 6'6", 218-pound freshman is devastating once he builds momentum, bullying smaller defenders and using his 6'11" wingspan to finish through traffic. His physical ceiling is substantial, but his jumper, pace control and overall point-guard polish remain developmental areas.

30.name: Brendon Kohl
30.about: The best shooter in the class, Kohl turned his junior season at Delaware into a showcase of elite perimeter shot-making. He’s dangerous spotting up, sprinting off screens or relocating into open space, while possessing the confidence and touch to convert heavily contested attempts. His shooting provides an immediate NBA-caliber skill, though expanding his off-the-dribble game and defensive impact would make him considerably more versatile.

31.name: Jaden Russo
31.about: A physically imposing veteran guard, Russo used his strength and downhill aggression to anchor Villanova’s backcourt as a senior. At 6'6" and 213 pounds, he can overpower smaller defenders, absorb contact around the basket and create advantages in transition while offering a respectable perimeter jumper. His age and limited finesse as a creator cap his upside, but his physicality gives him a clear NBA role-player pathway.

32.name: Jumon Peters
32.about: Relentless defensive pressure became Peters’ calling card during his senior season at Arkansas. Despite standing just 6'1", his strong 198-pound frame and 6'6" wingspan allow him to crowd ball handlers, fight through screens and create turnovers at the point of attack. He brings toughness and functional playmaking offensively, though inconsistent shooting limits his value away from the ball.

33.name: CeeCee Hayes
33.about: Few bigs in the class can match Hayes’ sheer combination of size, power and explosiveness. At 243 pounds, he generates violent finishes around the basket, overwhelms smaller frontcourts on the glass and gives USC an imposing lob target. His physical tools are enticing, but his limited shooting, raw offensive feel and reliance on athletic advantages make him a developmental frontcourt prospect.

34.name: Eugene Smith
34.about: A polished veteran scoring package made Smith the primary perimeter weapon at SMU. He’s comfortable attacking closeouts, rising into pull-ups or spacing the floor away from the ball, giving him multiple ways to contribute offensively. Limited burst and defensive range temper his ceiling, but his combination of shooting touch, strength and controlled creation gives him a strong second-round case.

35.name: Kazi Mwangaza
35.about: Mwangaza’s exceptional dimensions and defensive instincts give him a clear pathway to impacting games without needing offensive touches. His 7'5" wingspan makes him a constant deterrent around the basket, while his mobility allows him to cover ground as a help defender and recover for blocks. His offensive game remains extremely limited outside of rim running and putbacks, making further skill and strength development essential.

36.name: Mathias Béthuleau
36.about: Béthuleau offers an appealing blend of size and perimeter skill, using polished footwork and changes of pace to manufacture offense against professional competition. He can attack closeouts, create pull-ups and provide useful shooting at 6'8". Average athleticism and questions about his defensive impact complicate the projection, leaving his ability to consistently create separation as an important swing skill.

37.name: Kauã Menezes
37.about: Still early in his development, Menezes possesses an intriguing combination of size, length and perimeter skill that gives him long-term upside. He’s comfortable attacking closeouts and creating jumpers from the midrange, while occasionally flashing deeper range despite inconsistent results from three. His 6'11" wingspan provides defensive potential, but adding strength and becoming a more reliable shooter will be important to maximizing his NBA value.

38.name: Anthony Motley
38.about: Motley’s massive frame and emerging perimeter game make him an intriguing developmental center. At 7'2" with a 7'7" wingspan, he alters shots simply by occupying space around the rim and has enough mobility to recover as a help defender. His developing jumper adds another dimension offensively, though he remains relatively raw as a scorer and needs additional strength to consistently handle physical NBA centers.

39.name: Finn McMillan
39.about: A well-rounded offensive skill set and experience against professional competition make McMillan an intriguing big combo guard. He sees the floor well from either backcourt spot, creates effectively out of ball screens and can punish defenders with pull-up jumpers when given space. His lack of burst limits his separation and rim pressure, but his size, feel and versatility give him a viable NBA backup-guard pathway.

40.name: Ahmir Black
40.about: After transferring from Tennessee to Colorado, Black carved out a larger role through physicality, rebounding and relentless interior work. His powerful 240-pound frame allows him to establish deep position, clear space on the glass and finish through contact despite being undersized for an NBA big. His complete lack of perimeter shooting and average athleticism narrow his projection, putting considerable pressure on his rebounding and toughness to translate.

41.name: Terrell Santos
41.about: Length, shooting touch and finishing ability give Santos an intriguing developmental foundation after his freshman season at Tennessee. He can attack closeouts, cut into open space and finish above the rim while flashing legitimate spot-up potential. His thin frame and limited creation currently keep him in a complementary role, but there are enough tools for him to develop into a useful NBA forward.

42.name: Bradley Washington
42.about: Washington offers an unusual scoring profile for a 245-pound center, preferring to attack from the face-up game rather than simply operate around the rim. He uses a smooth midrange jumper, controlled drives and solid footwork to exploit slower bigs, while his length gives him tools to contribute defensively. His three-point range remains underdeveloped, and average athleticism limits his margin for error on both ends.

43.name: Matt Chaney
43.about: Chaney developed into a steady offensive organizer at Texas Tech, combining dependable perimeter shooting with patient pick-and-roll playmaking. He operates comfortably off ball screens, keeps defenses honest with his pull-up jumper and rarely gets sped up as a decision-maker. Limited athleticism restricts his finishing and defensive versatility, making his shooting and ability to run an offense central to his NBA value.

44.name: Eddy Suarez
44.about: By his senior season at Oklahoma, Suarez had developed into a productive veteran wing with a sturdy 218-pound frame, dependable perimeter scoring and enough athleticism to attack aggressive closeouts. He’s at his best spacing the floor, running off screens and taking advantage of mismatches with straight-line drives. His limited creation and playmaking lower his offensive ceiling, but his physical profile gives him multiple avenues to contribute as a complementary scorer.

45.name: Antonio Jefferson
45.about: Jefferson’s ability to operate as a 6'7" initiator gives him an unusual offensive profile. He sees cutters well, organizes possessions from multiple spots and can handle in transition while providing respectable perimeter shooting. The versatility is appealing, but his lack of burst and limited scoring pressure raise questions about whether his playmaking will be dynamic enough to warrant significant NBA creation responsibilities.

46.name: Kyson Barnes
46.about: Barnes brings an unusual combination of scoring craft and passing at 6'8", comfortably initiating offense and creating opportunities for teammates from several areas of the floor. His footwork and touch make him effective inside the arc, while his vision allows him to function as a secondary playmaker. Average athleticism and limited rim pressure could make translating his distinctive offensive style more challenging.

47.name: Yehuda Harrison
47.about: Harrison developed into a versatile frontcourt scorer at Utah, doing much of his best work attacking mismatches inside the arc. He uses his strong frame, footwork and touch to score from the mid-post, drive slower forwards and finish through contact, while showing enough passing feel to keep the offense moving. His lack of a standout NBA skill and inconsistent perimeter shooting make his eventual role less certain.

48.name: Leonardo Longo
48.about: Longo’s enormous frame gives him a natural defensive role as a traditional backline anchor. At 7'3", he uses positioning, verticality and sheer size to clog driving lanes, protect the basket and control the defensive glass without needing much athleticism. His severe mobility limitations and almost nonexistent perimeter game narrow his NBA fit, but his size and interior awareness provide a potential specialist role.

49.name: Brian Buckley
49.about: Buckley relies on strength, touch and an advanced mid-post game rather than athleticism to generate offense. The 255-pound freshman can establish position, turn over either shoulder and use an assortment of fakes and short jumpers to create quality looks. His scoring craft is intriguing, but poor mobility, limited rim protection and virtually no floor-spacing ability create significant questions about his NBA fit.

50.name: Max Estes
50.about: After spending his first three seasons at BYU, Estes transferred to Tennessee and immediately provided the Volunteers with an experienced shot-maker in the backcourt. His shifty handle, change of pace and pull-up shooting make him dangerous around ball screens, while he can also threaten defenses off the catch. His small frame and limited athleticism remain concerns, particularly defensively and finishing against NBA length.

51.name: Blake Christy
51.about: Few players in the class can rival Christy’s shooting ability, particularly when operating off screens and relocating without the ball. His sturdy frame and quick release give him a specialist pathway at the next level, but severe athletic limitations create substantial concerns defensively and around the basket. His NBA chances will largely depend on whether his shooting is exceptional enough to outweigh those limitations.

52.name: Will Ross Jr
52.about: Energy and vertical pop define Ross’ game on the wing, particularly when he can get downhill, cut behind defenses or run the floor in transition. He uses his 6'10" wingspan to finish around length and flashes defensive upside when engaged. His half-court skill set remains relatively raw, with continued development as a shooter and creator necessary to expand his role beyond an athletic complementary wing.

53.name: Josh Peters
53.about: Peters remains more projection than finished product, but his length and athleticism give him an appealing developmental foundation. He’s an active cutter, dangerous transition target and explosive finisher who can create easy offense without needing touches. Encouraging spot-up flashes offer additional upside, though his handle, shooting consistency and self-creation will need significant development for him to earn a dependable NBA role.

54.name: Eddie Thomas
54.about: Thomas brings a physical but surprisingly skilled presence to Arkansas’ frontcourt, using his 240-pound frame to establish position, control the glass and score through contact. He’s also a capable passer from the post, recognizing cutters and finding open shooters when defenses collapse. His limited length and athleticism create defensive concerns, but his rebounding, interior playmaking and developing jumper give him several ways to contribute.

55.name: Myles Browne
55.about: Browne brings an aggressive two-way mentality to the backcourt, using a tight handle and quick pull-up game to manufacture offense while consistently disrupting opposing guards defensively. His long 6'7" wingspan helps compensate for his 6'2" frame, particularly in passing lanes. The jumper remains streaky, however, and his scoring efficiency can suffer when he settles for difficult isolation attempts.

56.name: Tyler Gibbons
56.about: Gibbons made his presence felt as a freshman through energy, athleticism and relentless work on the offensive glass. His quick second jump allows him to extend possessions and turn misses into finishes, while his 7'0" wingspan helps compensate for being undersized for an NBA interior role. His offensive skill set remains extremely limited away from the basket, making his development as a defender and finisher critical to his chances of sticking.

57.name: Elijah Andrews
57.about: Andrews creates much of his value through activity, athleticism and intelligent off-ball movement rather than advanced creation. He cuts hard, runs the floor and uses his strong frame to finish through traffic while contributing on the glass. There are useful complementary tools here, but his limited handle and playmaking leave him dependent on teammates to generate much of his offense.

58.name: Caleb Jordan
58.about: An explosive downhill guard, Jordan emerged as a productive senior behind his ability to attack gaps and put consistent pressure on the rim. His strong 196-pound frame helps him absorb contact despite standing just 6'0", and he can provide energy in transition and at the point of attack defensively. At 24, however, his limited shooting and modest playmaking ceiling leave little margin for error as an NBA prospect.

59.name: Matt Weber
59.about: Tasked with carrying a significant creation burden at The Citadel, Weber proved capable of balancing perimeter shooting with playmaking responsibilities. He’s comfortable working off ball screens, finding teammates when defenses commit and spacing the floor from deep. His combination of size and feel is appealing, but limited athleticism raises concerns about separation, finishing and defending NBA guards.

60.name: Elijah Walters
60.about: Versatility is the foundation of Walters’ offensive game, allowing him to contribute as a cutter, transition scorer and secondary ball handler rather than relying on one dominant skill. He uses changes of pace and touch to create opportunities inside the arc and has enough shooting ability to keep defenses honest. His unusual lack of length and inconsistent perimeter impact on both ends limit his margin for error as an NBA prospect.

61.name: George Tămaș
61.about: Tămaș has built his game around physical rebounding and touch inside the arc, giving Dinamo București a dependable frontcourt presence. He’s comfortable stepping into midrange jumpers, scoring off short rolls and using positioning to compensate for modest athletic tools. His lack of ideal size, explosiveness and three-point range creates questions about how cleanly his game translates to the NBA.

62.name: Daouda Ndao
62.about: Ndao is a long-term developmental gamble centered around exceptional length and defensive upside. His 7'3" wingspan gives him legitimate shot-blocking and switching potential, while he can finish opportunistically around the basket. His offensive skill level remains extremely raw and his thin frame needs considerable development, making him more of a tools-based project than someone prepared for immediate NBA minutes.

63.name: Jonathan Patterson
63.about: Patterson flashes an appealing pull-up scoring package at 6'7", using controlled footwork and changes of pace to manufacture jumpers inside the arc. There are moments where his size and shot-making hint at greater offensive potential, but consistency remains elusive. Average athleticism, limited strength and uneven efficiency make him a developmental scoring wing who will need to prove he can contribute beyond difficult shot-making.

64.name: Vedran Vlahović
64.about: Vlahović offers intriguing positional versatility as a 6'7" ball handler who can initiate offense, attack mismatches and create looks from the midrange. He plays with good pace and uses his size effectively against smaller guards, but remains more comfortable inside the arc than as a perimeter shooter. Improving his three-point consistency and adding strength will be critical to carving out an NBA role.

65.name: Alec Meeks
65.about: Comfortable operating as a complementary piece, Meeks settled into a valuable role at Duke by providing floor spacing and dependable perimeter defense without requiring many touches. His 6'9" wingspan helps him bother opposing guards and wings, while his left-handed jumper makes him a reliable catch-and-shoot threat. Limited self-creation and playmaking restrict his ceiling, but his straightforward 3-and-D skill set gives him a realistic role-player pathway.

66.name: Timothy Sykes
66.about: Sykes is a crafty half-court guard who relies on footwork, touch and change of pace rather than physical advantages. He’s comfortable creating pull-ups from the midrange, navigating ball screens and getting defenders off balance before finding his shot. His skill level gives him developmental appeal, but limited size, length and athleticism create significant questions about his defensive viability and finishing at the NBA level.

67.name: Toby Farnsworth
67.about: Farnsworth developed into a useful floor-spacing big during his UConn career, using his height and high release point to get jumpers off cleanly against opposing centers. He’s comfortable popping into open space and provides enough interior size to contribute on the glass. His modest shooting efficiency, average mobility and limited interior presence leave him without a standout NBA skill, however, making him a fringe developmental option.

68.name: Bryson McDowell
68.about: After transferring from Cal to UCLA for his senior season, McDowell provided the Bruins with an experienced, physical ball handler capable of creating offense inside the arc. His strong frame, long arms and creative finishing package help him convert from difficult angles, while he can facilitate when defenses collapse. An inconsistent jumper and tendency to over-dribble limit his effectiveness away from the ball.

69.name: Dante Zárate
69.about: Zárate’s enormous dimensions allow him to remain productive despite being one of the least athletic prospects in the class. He uses his 7'7" wingspan to alter shots, clean up misses and generate second-chance points while rarely venturing away from the basket. His extremely limited mobility makes defending in space a major concern, leaving him projected as a situational interior specialist.

70.name: Toby Jansen
70.about: Jansen carved out a productive role at Virginia with strength, touch and an unconventional offensive game for his size. He uses his 238-pound frame to punish smaller wings, can step outside for occasional threes and shows craft attacking mismatches from the perimeter or post. His tweener dimensions and average athleticism make the NBA fit difficult, however, leaving him without an obvious defensive matchup.

71.name: Destin Bryant
71.about: Bryant is a methodical shot-creating guard who does his best work manipulating defenders in the half court. He uses hesitations, footwork and a polished pull-up game to manufacture space, while showing enough passing feel to operate the pick-and-roll. His lack of standout size or athleticism lowers his margin for error, and he’ll need to become a more consistent three-point shooter to stick at the NBA level.

72.name: Trey Raymond Jr
72.about: Raymond carved out a dependable role at Oregon by providing size, physicality and disciplined interior defense. He understands positioning, stays vertical around the basket and uses his 248-pound frame to hold ground against opposing centers while contributing on the glass. His poor mobility and extremely limited offensive range restrict his NBA upside, projecting him primarily as a depth big who can provide situational interior defense.

73.name: Matt Hanson
73.about: Hanson’s shooting touch gives him a chance to overcome an otherwise limited physical profile. He’s comfortable stepping into pick-and-pop threes, spacing beyond the arc and using his 253-pound frame to set sturdy screens. His severe athletic limitations are difficult to hide defensively, however, particularly in space, making his ability to consistently stretch the floor essential to earning an NBA role.

74.name: Eduardo Cifuentes
74.about: Cifuentes built his value at Ohio State around physicality, positioning and an old-school interior game. He uses his strong 243-pound frame to carve out space on the glass, establish deep post position and convert through contact with solid touch. His combination of age, limited size and almost nonexistent perimeter game significantly restricts his NBA ceiling, but his toughness and rebounding could earn him opportunities as a depth big.

75.name: Tyson Owens
75.about: Owens emerged as a productive senior floor general at Grand Canyon, balancing scoring responsibilities with steady creation for teammates. He’s comfortable operating out of ball screens, can knock down pull-ups when defenders go under and generally keeps the offense organized. Without standout size, shooting or athleticism, however, he projects as a fringe draft prospect who will need his decision-making to separate him.
